## Overview

Proportional symbol maps (also known as graduated symbol maps) use the visual variable of **size** to represent differences in the magnitude of a discrete phenomenon. For example, counts of people or number of wins. In this exercise, an interactive proportional symbol map is created showing the number of wins by Singapore Pools outlets, using the `tmap` package in R.

## Reflections

What stood out in this exercise was the difference between `tmap_mode("plot")` and `tmap_mode("view")`, switching to view mode turns the map into a fully interactive Leaflet map in the browser. Being able to encode two variables simultaneously — size for the number of wins and colour for the outlet type — in a single proportional symbol map makes it far more informative than a basic dot map. The `sync = TRUE` argument in `tm_facets()` was particularly impressive: it keeps the zoom and pan of two separate maps synchronised, making comparison intuitive.

## Getting Started

### Loading Packages


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)
```
:::


## Data Wrangling

### Importing the Data


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sgpools <- read_csv("SGPools_svy21.csv")
list(sgpools)
```
:::


The dataset contains 306 Singapore Pools outlets with their x/y coordinates in SVY21 projection (EPSG: 3414).

### Converting to a Simple Feature Data Frame


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# st_as_sf() converts a data frame with coordinate columns into a spatial sf object
sgpools_sf <- st_as_sf(sgpools,
                       coords = c("XCOORD", "YCOORD"),
                       crs = 3414)
list(sgpools_sf)
```
:::


**Key arguments:**

-   `coords` takes the column name for the x-coordinate first, then the y-coordinate
-   `crs = 3414` is the EPSG code for Singapore's SVY21 coordinate system
-   A new `geometry` column is added with the point coordinates

## Drawing Proportional Symbol Maps

### Switching to Interactive Mode


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tmap_mode("view")
```
:::


### Basic Point Symbol Map


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = 1,
             col  = "black",
             lwd  = 1)
```
:::


### Making It Proportional


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Size is now proportional to the number of wins
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "red",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col  = "black",
             lwd  = 1)
```
:::


Assigning a numerical variable to `size` makes the symbol area proportional to the value — larger bubbles = more wins.

### Encoding a Second Variable with Colour


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Size = winnings, Colour = outlet type
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col  = "black",
             lwd  = 1)
```
:::


Two variables are encoded at once: size for the quantity of wins and colour for the outlet category.

### Synchronised Faceted Map


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# sync = TRUE keeps zoom and pan in sync across facets
tm_shape(sgpools_sf) +
  tm_bubbles(fill = "OUTLET TYPE",
             size = "Gp1Gp2 Winnings",
             col  = "black",
             lwd  = 1) +
  tm_facets(by   = "OUTLET TYPE",
            nrow = 1,
            sync = TRUE)
```
:::


`tm_facets()` splits the map by outlet type. With `sync = TRUE`, zooming or panning one map automatically updates the other, which is very useful for direct spatial comparison.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Switch back to static mode at end of session
tmap_mode("plot")
```
:::
